Interpretation: A SRSF2 p.P95R missense variant was identified. This variant alters binding properties of exonic motifs in the SRSF2 protein product, resulting in aberrant splicing of key hematopoietic regulators and impaired hematopoietic differentiation (PMID: 31040863, 25965569). This alteration is a well-characterized mutational hotspot, predicted to be likely oncogenic, and has been reported by COSMIC in chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) (COSM211661). Missense mutations in the SRSF2 codon 95 are reported in 40% of CMML cases and are associated with poor prognosis (NCCN, MDS v1.2023). Furthermore, SRSF2 mutations have been detected in 38% of CMML samples (PMID: 22588877, 23550210). The management of CMML depends on the characteristics of the patient's disease and is typically focused on supportive care and cytoreductive therapy (NCCN, MDSv1.2023). The WHO classification of hematological malignancies indicates that the presence of mutations in genes often associated with CMML (including SRSF2) can be used to support a diagnosis in the proper clinical context. Mutations in SRSF2 can be helpful adjunct studies in difficult cases, particularly given the normal karyotype of CMML. However, this should not be used alone as proof of neoplasia as mutations can occur in healthy, older individuals as clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP). Therefore, caution should be used in the interpretation of these genetic results (PMID: 27069254). SRSF2 encodes a member of the Serine/Arginine (SR)-rich family of pre-mRNA splicing factors, which constitute a part of the spliceosome complex. These pre-mRNA splicing factors bind RNA through their RRM motif and other proteins via the RS domain, which facilitates interaction between different SR splicing factors. SRSF2 is essential for mRNA splicing, nuclear mRNA export, protein translation and hematopoiesis (PMID: 26124281).

A CBL p.C396G missense variant was identified. This variant resides in the functional RING finger domain, likely affecting gene product function and may potentially contribute to inactivation and/or tumorigenesis (PMID: 28481359, PMID: 21828135). While this specific variant has been reported by COSMIC (COSM34074, Oct 2022) in chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML), it has not been reported in ClinVar. However, a different non-synonymous, missense mutation, in the same CBL 396 codon, is reported as pathogenic in Noonan syndrome-like disorder with juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (Variation ID: 29823). The presence of a CBL p.C396G variant is indicative of an unfavorable prognosis in patients diagnosed with CMML (NCCN, MDSv1.2023).     CBL is altered in ~15% of CMML cases (PMID: 31736132). CBL missense mutations (in codons 366-420) are commonly found in CMML (10-20%) (NCCN, MDS v1.2023). Additionally, CBL mutations have demonstrated adverse prognostic impact and association with inferior overall survival in patients diagnosed with CMML (PMID: 26230957, 23690417). The hypomethylating agents azacitidine and decitabine, inhibitors of DNA methyltransferases, have demonstrated efficacy for patients with CMML. CBL is a proto-oncogene and its protein product functions as an E3 ubiquitin-ligase that mediates degradation of receptor tyrosine kinases (PMID: 11283727, 23085373, 28611190). CBL family E3 ligases selectively and negatively regulate activated receptor tyrosine kinases, including EGFR (PMID: 23085373), PDGFR (PMID: 11283727), CSF-1R (PMID: 11283727), MET (PMID: 24384534) and FLT3 (PMID: 17446348), through ubiquitylation that targets these proteins for proteasomal degradation (PMID: 11283727). The activity of CBL is required to negatively regulate various signaling pathways, most commonly in hematopoietic and immune cells (PMID: 11857085).

A GATA2 p.K390E missense variant was identified. This specific variant resides in the functional ZF-2 domain, likely affecting gene product function and has been reported as likely pathogenic by ClinVar in GATA2 deficiency with susceptibility to MDS/AML, Deafness-lymphedema-leukemia (Variation ID: 1184011). Additionally, this variant has been reported by COSMIC in myelofibrosis and chronic myeloid leukemia (COSM1235009). GATA2 is a transcription factor that functions as a master regulator of hematopoietic differentiation. GATA2 activates the expression of genes essential to hematopoiesis, including those involved in stem cell maintenance and cell specification (PMID: 8078582, 12433372, 25578878, 20887958, 28481359). Appropriate expression of GATA2 is required in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells to initiate hematopoietic lineage specification (PMID: 28179280). In MDS patients, GATA2 mutations (including frameshift, nonsense, splice site and missense in codons 349-398) are associated with poor prognosis (NCCN, MDS v1.2023). Genetic lesions occurring in GATA2 have been implicated in familial cases of MDS and other myeloid malignancies. These are included under the 'myeloid neoplasms with germline GATA2 mutation' WHO classification (NCCN, MDS v1.2023, PMID: 27069254). GATA2 encodes for a transcription factor which contains the highly-conserved zing finger domains, essential to the DNA-binding ability of the GATA2 protein (PMID: 11262875). This allows for binding of consensus nucleotide sequences in promoter regions of target genes, resulting in the protein acting as a master regulator in transcription of genes involved in the development and proliferation of hematopoietic lineages (PMID 24371770, 32960960).

A TET2 c.3595-2A>G splice site variant was identified. This intronic substitution is predicted to affect mRNA splicing and result in either exon skipping or the inclusion of introns, likely altering protein function. TET2 is involved in myelopoiesis and alterations in the TET2 gene are associated with several myeloproliferative disorders. While the TET2 c.3595-2A>G variant is located in a 3' canonical splice acceptor site, this variant has not been reported by COSMIC and its functional impact has not been characterized. Azacitidine and decitabine, both inhibitors of DNA methyltransferases, are FDA-approved for treating patients diagnosed with CMML. In patients diagnosed with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), including chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML), that have more than one genetic mutation in TET2, treatment with azacitidine has been shown to be associated with a higher response rate compared to those with wild-type TET2 (PMID: 29291002). While TET2 mutations have been show to impact the response to hypomethylating agents, TET2 genetic alteration status had no effect on the overall survival of CMML patients who have been treated with hypomethylating agents (NCCN, MDSv1.2023, PMID: 30964202). TET2 splice site mutations have been associated with a worsened overall prognosis and an increased rate of leukemic transformation in patients diagnosed with MDS (NCCN, MDS v1.2023).

A FLT3 internal tandem duplication (ITD) alteration (p.Y597_E598ins23) was detected. The FLT3 (FMS-like tyrosine kinase 3) gene encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase that regulates hematopoiesis and leads to activation of key signaling pathways related to cell growth and survival, including MAPK, JAK-STAT, and PI3K (PMID: 21453545, 19549778). FLT3 driver mutations occur in approximately 30% of all AML cases (PMID: 30651634). FLT3-ITD mutations, the most common type, are associated with constitutive activation of the FLT3 protein. Numerous studies have shown the negative prognostic influence of FLT3-ITD in patients with AML, resulting in shorter remission durations (eg, decreased disease-free survival in patients with a complete remission) and poorer survival outcomes compared with patients who have wild-type FLT3. A study reported that FLT3-mutated AML patients had a higher risk of relapse post-stem cell transplant compared to wild-type patients. However, FLT3 mutation status was not significantly associated with leukemia-free survival or overall survival (PMID: 27315441).    Please see the most recent NCCN guidelines (v2.2022) for Acute Myeloid Leukemia for combination treatment recommendations for patients with a FLT3 -ITD mutation.

A RUNX1 p.E80Gfs*58 frameshift variant was detected. This variant is a premature termination mutation and therefore likely associated with loss of function. RUNX1 encodes the DNA binding subunit of a highly conserved transcription factor (Core-binding factor, CBF) that regulates hematopoietic differentiation, and acts as a transcriptional activator or repressor in a context-dependent manner (PMID: 26483790). RUNX1-mutated AML is associated with a complex mutation cluster, often co-occurring with mutations in epigenetic modifiers and/or spliceosome complex genes. In univariable analyses, RUNX1 mutations were associated with inferior event-free, relapse-free, and overall survival in all patients (PMID: 27137476). In AML patients (n = 1540) with mutations in chromatin-spliceosome group genes (including RUNX1 and SRSF2), the patients were older, with lower white-cell and blast counts, lower rates of response to induction chemotherapy, higher relapse rates, and a poor long-term clinical outlook as compared with patients in other subgroups (PMID: 27276561).

A SRSF2 p.P95H missense mutation was identified. Codon P95 in SRSF2 is a hotspot, and mutations (including p.P95H) have been shown to cause mis-splicing of key hematopoietic regulators and impaired hematopoietic differentiation (PMID: 25965569). The SRSF2 gene encodes a member of the Serine/Arginine (SR)-rich family of pre-mRNA splicing factors, which constitute a part of the spliceosome complex. The presence of mutations in genes including SRSF2 was reported to be >95% specific for the diagnosis of secondary AML (sAML) compared with de novo AML (PMID: 25550361). In a recent study of 2,678 patients, mutations in splicing factor genes (including SRSF2) were associated with inferior relapse-free and overall survival, however these mutations did not represent independent prognostic markers (PMID: 32358566). In AML patients treated with frontline hypomethylating agents and venetoclax–based therapy, spliceosome mutations (including SRSF2) had no impact on overall survival or composite complete response (PMID: 33885753).

A TET2, p.K147*,nonsense mutation was identified. TET2 p.K147* is expected to result in a premature truncation and a loss-of-function of protein. TET2 p.K147* is neither reported nor functionally characterized in the literature. TET2 is a DNA demethylase that functions as a tumor suppressor. Defects in this gene have been associated with several hematologic malignancies (PMID: 26099018). The therapeutic significance of TET2 mutation in AML is not clear. In high-risk AML (age range 60-86 years), TET2 mutations did not impact median overall survival, disease-free survival and complete remission (CR) rates in patients treated with decitabine in combination with low-dose cytarabine, aclarubicin, and G-CSF (D-CAG) (PMID: 32238611). As per a study in AML patients treated with hypomethylating agents (HMAs) in both the frontline and relapsed/refractory setting, TET2 mutations had no impact on clinical response to the HMAs (PMID: 27418649). In elderly AML patients (Age 65-90y) treated in the FLUGAZA phase III clinical trial comparing azacytidine (AZA) with fludarabine plus low-dose cytarabine (FLUGA), increased TET2 mutant variant allele frequency (VAF) was associated with higher overall response rate after the third cycle of azacytidine [VAF distribution is responders vs non-responders in both treatment arms [AZA arm, VAF-TET2 (20% vs. 8.7% respectively) (PMID: 34070172).

A DNMT3A p.R882H missense variant was detected. Codon 882 is a mutational hotspot that lies within the SAM-dependent C-terminal catalytic methyltransferase (C5-type) domain of the DNMT3A (UniProt.org). R882 is the most commonly mutated residue. DNMT3A R882H results in approximately 80% reduction of the methyltransferase activity (PMID: 24656771). This mutation has also been observed in conjunction with NPM1 mutations and FLT3 mutations.     DNMT3A encodes a DNA methyltransferase that is essential for the establishment of DNA methylation patterns during development (PMID: 25693834). DNMT3A mutations have been reported in 18% to 22% of patients with AML. Data concerning the prognostic significance of DNMT3A mutations have thus far been conflicting. Some studies in the overall AML population and in patients with intermediate risk reported no significant effect of DNMT3A mutations on survival outcomes, whereas other studies have shown a negative prognostic effect in the overall population or specific subgroups.

A TP53 p.P278L missense variant was identified. The p.P278L mutation resides in the DNA-binding domain of TP53 and has been shown to result in loss of transactivation activity in vitro (PMID: 22713868, 16861262). This variant is associated with unfavorable prognosis in MDS (NCCN, MDS v1.2023, PMID: 24836762, 21220588, 25092778). Patients diagnosed with MDS who harbor TP53 mutations have been reported to respond well to decitabine (PMID: 27959731). Somatic TP53 variants are frequently observed in a variety of malignancies, including MDS, where it is associated with poor prognosis and may predict resistance or relapse to lenalidomide (NCCN, MDS v1.2023). Additionally, mutations in TP53 have been shown to predict decreased overall survival in multivariable models adjusted for IPSS or IPSS-R risk groups in several studies of distinct cohorts (NCCN, MDS v1.2023). The TP53 gene product acts as a tumor suppressor by regulating expression of target genes via induction of cell cycle arrest, senescence, apoptosis and DNA repair (PMID: 22294769, 20182602). If DNA repair is not an amenable option, the TP53 gene product can prevent DNA-damaged cells from dividing and signal them to undergo apoptosis, ultimately preventing tumor development (PMID: 10065147, 22713868).

A TP53 p.V173M missense variant was identified. This variant is located in the functional DNA-binding domain and may affect TP53 function and is associated with unfavorable prognosis in myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) (NCCN, MDS v1.2023, PMID: 24836762, 21220588, 25092778). While the TP53 p.V173M mutation has been reported by COSMIC in several myeloid and lymphoid malignancies, it has not been reported in MDS (COSM11084). Patients diagnosed with MDS who harbor TP53 mutations have been reported to respond well to decitabine (PMID: 27959731). Somatic TP53 variants are frequently observed in a variety of malignancies, including MDS, where it is associated with poor prognosis and may predict resistance or relapse to lenalidomide (NCCN, MDS v1.2023). Additionally, mutations in TP53 have been shown to predict decreased overall survival in multivariable models adjusted for IPSS or IPSS-R risk groups in several studies of distinct cohorts (NCCN, MDS v1.2023). The TP53 gene product acts as a tumor suppressor by regulating expression of target genes via induction of cell cycle arrest, senescence, apoptosis and DNA repair (PMID: 22294769, 20182602). If DNA repair is not an amenable option, the TP53 gene product can prevent DNA-damaged cells from dividing and signal them to undergo apoptosis, ultimately preventing tumor development (PMID: 10065147, 22713868).

A JAK2 p.V617F activating mutation was identified. JAK2 gain-of-function alterations occur in up to 50% of MDS/MPN-RS-T patients (PMID: 33428785). JAK2 encodes a receptor-associated Janus kinase that plays a central role in cytokine and growth factor signaling. Codon 617 lies within the pseudo-protein tyrosine kinase domain (PMID: 34095761) and results in constitutive activation of JAK2 and its downstream signaling pathways (PMID: 15858187). Please note JAK2 p.V617F mutations have been found in older individuals that exhibit clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminant potential (CHIP) (PMID: 31672865).    Please refer to the most recent version of NCCN guidelines (v1.2023) for Myelodysplastic Syndromes for treatment recommendations for MDS/MPN-RS-T.

A SF3B1, K700E, missense variant was identified. SF3B1 (splicing factor 3b subunit 1) is a component of the spliceosome complex that regulates the removal of introns from messenger RNA. Codon K700 is a mutational hotspot located in one of the 22 HEAT (HEAT 5) repeat domains, which mediates SF3B1 interaction with other proteins, RNA, and is the site of ubiquitination, an important regulator of function and protein stability (PMID: 26842708). SF3B1 p.K700E has been shown to result in deregulated splicing at a subset of junctions, driving differential gene expression, primarily by the use of an alternative 3'-splice site (PMID:27524419, 26842708). SF3B1 mutations are strongly associated with the presence of ring sideroblasts, and are highly prevalent in patients with MDS-RS or MDS-RS-T (>80%). According to 2016 WHO classification of myeloid neoplasms, a diagnosis of MDS/MPN-RS-T is strongly supported by the presence of SF3B1 mutation together with a mutation in JAK2 V617F, CALR, or MPL genes (PMID: 27069254). The International Working Group for the Prognosis of Myelodysplastic Syndromes (IWG-PM) proposed a new subtype of myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) characterized by somatic mutations in SF3B1: MDS with mutated SF3B1. The group is characterized by optional presence of ring sideroblasts, cytopenia, somatic SF3B1 mutations, isolated erythroid or multilineage dysplasia, <5% BM blasts, <1% PRBL blasts, and not meeting classic criteria for MDS or MDS/MPN (PMID: 32645165). The updated WHO classification expanded the definition of MDS-RS to include patients who have the SF3B1 mutation but lack excess blasts or an isolated del(5q) abnormality. The frequency of spliceosome gene SF3B1 mutations in up to 60% of MDS-RS-T cases has resulted in the inclusion of MDS/MPN RS-T as a full entity. Typical mutations in other genes can also establish the presence of clonal hematopoiesis, but they are less specific for disease subtype. Of note, several mutated genes associated with MDS (e.g., TET2, DNMT3A, SF3B1, EZH2, NRAS, BRAF, TP53) can be mutated in other neoplasms, including lymphoid malignancies. Rare patients can have dual diagnoses (e.g., MDS and chronic lymphocytic leukemia), which can confound the interpretation of sequencing results. Therefore, the presence of mutations must be interpreted in an appropriate clinical context consistent with MDS. Mutated SF3B1 variant allele frequency (VAF) greater than or equal to 10% or greater than or equal to 15% ring sideroblasts (RS) may substitute for SF3B1 mutation (MDS with low blasts and ring sideroblasts) (NCCN, v1.2023). Please refer to the most recent version of NCCN guidelines for Myelodysplastic Syndromes for treatment recommendations for MDS/MPN-RS-T.

A STAG2 p.K584Rfs*2 frameshift, premature terminating mutation was identified. Nonsense, frameshift or splice site mutations in the STAG2 gene occur in 5-10% myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and are associated with poor prognosis (NCCN v1.2023). STAG2 is a subunit of the cohesin complex and its targeted inactivation results in chromatid cohesion defects and aneuploidy. This mutation is expected to cause loss of regulatory phosphorylation sites and loss-of-function of the protein (PMID: 26871722). In a large whole-exome and/or targeted sequencing study of MDS patients, STAG2 mutations were significantly enriched in high-risk MDS (in comparison to low-risk MDS) (PMID: 27992414). In MDS patients, STAG2 mutations tended to associate with multilineage dysplasia or an excess blast and their presence was independently associated with adverse outcomes in MDS patients (PMID: 29515765; 24850867; 28220884). The presence of a STAG2 mutation is independently associated with adverse overall survival, particularly in those classified as lower-risk by IPSS, but did not predict for shorter leukemia-free survival (Ref: http://www.bloodjournal.org/content/128/22/3182). In a study of patients with MDS and MDS/MPN treated with hypomethylating agents, patients with 3 or more mutations (including ASXL1, RUNX1 and, STAG2) were associated a lower likelihood of achieving response to therapy, with a shorter median response duration and shorter median overall survival (PMID: 29515765). Additionally, mutations in 3 or more genes including ASXL1, RUNX1 and STAG2 were associated with shorter time to AML progression (Ref- https://www.clinical-lymphoma-myeloma-leukemia.com/article/S2152-2650(18)30921-2/abstract).

An ASXL1 p.G646Wfs*12 premature terminating frameshift mutation was identified. ASXL1 is a member of the polycomb group of proteins, which are necessary for the maintenance of stable repression of homeotic and other loci. ASXL1 nonsense or frameshift mutations are found in 15-25% of MDS patients (NCCN, MDS v1. 2023). G646Wfs*12, located in the last exon, is expected to result in a premature termination and loss of the C-terminal histone/DNA-binding plant homeodomain (PHD) (PMID: 19609284). Mutations resulting in the deletion of the PHD domain of ASXL1 result in a loss-of-function (Blood (2012) 120 (21): 2393. Abstract 602). ASXL1 G646Wfs*12 is one of the most frequently identified mutations in AML patients (PMID: 25596267) and is also reported in MDS and PMF (PMID: 24030381, 26714837). ASXL1 frameshift mutations are associated with a poor prognosis in MDS (NCCN, MDS v1.2023; PMID: 21576631, 24442206).    FDA-approved treatments for MDS include hypomethylating agents (HMA), 5-azacitidine that are approved for all IPSS risk patients and decitabine which is approved for intermediate-1 or higher IPSS risk patients. In the setting of MDS, there is conflicting data regarding the efficacy of azacitidine and decitabine in patients with ASXL1 mutations. In a recent study in patients with higher-risk MDS, who were treated with azacitidine, mutations in histone modulators (e.g. ASXL1) were associated with prolonged survival (PMID:26959885). However, in an earlier study in patients with myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), who had received 5-azacyitidine, decitabine or both, better overall survival (OS) was associated with wild-type ASXL1 (PMID: 24045501); in the same cohort, this study also reported improved OS in patients harboring SF3B1 mutations.

A TET2 c.5269delC frameshift mutation was detected (NM_001127208.2) alternatively known as c.*5331+33008delC (NM_017628.4). This single nucleotide deletion mutation is expected to result in a premature truncation of the protein product denoted as p.H1757Ifs*6. TET2 is a DNA demethylase and functions as a tumor suppressor and defects in this gene have been associated with several hematological malignancies (PMID: 26099018). This alteration is upstream of the second conserved catalytic double-stranded beta-helix domain and is expected to result in partial loss of the catalytic function of the protein (PMID: 25132561). The p.H1757fs*6 variant has previously been reported in COSMIC (COSV54431737; PMID: 24413737). Recent meta-analysis studies in MDS patients reported that TET2 mutations had no significant impact on overall survival of MDS patients (PMID: 28476038, 28521175). TET2 mutations in MDS patients have been shown to be associated with a significantly higher response rate to azacitidine compared with wild-type TET2 (NCCN, MDS v.1.2023). Mutations in TET2 are independently associated with shorter overall survival after treatment with stem cell transplantation in MDS patients (PMID: 25961778; 25092778).

A RUNX1 p.S424Afs frame-shift mutation was identified. This four base pair insertion is predicted to cause an out of frame extension of the protein product denoted as p.Ser424Alafs*177. Runt-related transcription factor 1 (RUNX1) acts as a transcriptional activator or repressor in a context-dependent manner regulating hematopoietic differentiation (PMID: 14556655, 26483790, 28179279, 34111109). RUNX1 mutations are identified in 10% to 15% of MDS patients (NCCN, MDS v1.2023). Nonsense or Frameshift mutations in RUNX1 are independently associated with a poor prognosis in MDS.

A CBL, c.1096-1G>C, splice site mutation was identified. The mutation eliminates a splice acceptor site at the intron 7 – exon 8 boundary and is presumed to result in aberrant splicing and loss of function of the critical E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase RING finger domain. This variant is not found in the gnomAD population database but is listed in ClinVar as pathogenic (VarID: 180815) and found in individuals with a Noonan or Noonan-like syndrome with or without JMML (PMID: 25358541). Experimental studies have shown that this splice variant disrupts the canonical splice site and causes the in-frame skipping of exon 8 (PMID: 25952305). CBL (Casitas B-lineage lymphoma) is an E3 ubiquitin-ligase and proto-oncogene that mediates degradation of receptor tyrosine kinases (PMID: 23085373). CBL family E3 ligases selectively and negatively regulate activated receptor tyrosine kinases, including EGFR (PMID: 23085373), PDGFR (PMID: 11283727), CSF-1R (PMID: 11283727), MET (PMID: 24384534), and FLT3 (PMID: 17446348), through ubiquitylation that targets these proteins for degradation by the proteasome (PMID: 11283727). In myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) patients, mutated genes including CBL have been associated with shorter survival (PMID: 29618722).

An EZH2 p.C700Y missense variant was detected. This variant is located in the SET functional domain. This variant is not listed in dbSNP, ClinVar, COSMIC or gnomAD population frequency database. Nonsense and frameshift EZH2 mutations are associated with unfavorable prognosis in MDS and MDS/MPN, AML (NCCN, MDSv1.2023, PMID: 27276561). EZH2 encodes the catalytic component of the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), which is responsible for the methylation of lysine 27 on the N-terminal tail of histone H3 (H3K27) and influences stem cell renewal. Point mutations, resulting in gain-of-function, and inactivating mutations, have been reported in lymphoma and leukemia, suggest that EZH2 may serve a dual purpose as an oncogene and tumor-suppressor gene (PMID: 24097338). In myeloid neoplasms, mutations were found throughout EZH2 and have been described in 10-13% of poor-prognosis myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms (MDS/MPN), 13% of myelofibrosis (MF), 6% of MDS, and less frequently in acute myeloid leukemia (1.8%). EZH2 mutations were observed more frequently in cases with -7/del(7q) than in cases without -7/del(7q).    Hi Michel - I can find no glaring clinical information regarding missense mutations in EZH2. This is likely a tier III VOUS.

A RUNX1 p.Q286* premature terminating nonsense mutation was identified. Runt-related transcription factor 1 (RUNX1) acts as a transcriptional activator or repressor in a context-dependent manner regulating hematopoietic differentiation (PMID: 14556655, 26483790, 28179279, 34111109). RUNX1 mutations are identified in 10% to 15% of MDS patients (NCCN, MDS v1.2023). Codon 286 lies upstream of the proline/serine/threonine rich region at the C-terminus of RUNX1 which is necessary for transcriptional activation of target genes. RUNX1 p.Q286* is expected to result a the loss of function. RUNX1 p.Q286* has been not been reported in the literature and is not listed in ClinVar but has been observed in COSMIC (COSV55869697). RUNX1 nonsense and frameshift mutations are reported to be independently associated with a poor prognosis in MDS and may be familial in very rare cases (NCCN, MDS v3.2022). For patients with MDS/AML and MDS, somatic mutations in RUNX1 are independently associated with unfavorable outcomes and shorter survival after allogeneic HSCT (PMID: 27601546; NCCN MDS v1.2023).

A SRSF2, p.P95H, missense variant was identified. SRSF2 regulates spliceosomal components at both the 5'- and 3'-prime splice sites during spliceosome assembly. Codon 95 of SRSF2 is a mutational hot spot and genomic alterations may result in mis-splicing of key hematopoietic regulators and impaired hematopoietic differentiation (PMID: 25965569). Mutations in SRSF2 have been reported in chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML), as well as myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), myelofibrosis MF, and mastocytosis (PMID: 25445211, 22431577). The p.P95H variant of SRSF2 has been reported in COSMIC (COSV57969816) in CMML. Codon 95 missense mutations in SRSF2 are associated with poor prognosis (NCCN, MDS v1.2023). The p.P95H alteration has been shown to result in a gain of function, altering RNA-binding affinity and specificity of the SRSF2 RNA recognition motif (PMID: 25965569, 26261309). Pharmacologic modulation of splicing may offer potential treatments for tumors harboring spliceosomal mutations (PMID: 27836865).

A TET2, p.R1896S, missense variant was identified. TET2 is a DNA demethylase and functions as a tumor suppressor. Alterations in TET2 have been associated with several hematological malignancies (PMID: 26099018). Codon 1896 resides in the catalytic double-strand beta helix (DSBH) domain of TET2 and while p.R1896S is reported as a hypomorphic mutation and results in partial loss of function compared to wild-type TET2 in vitro, the functional impact of TET2 p.R1896S remains to be determined (PMID: 24697267, 25132561, 28130413). TET2 p.R1896S has been reported by COSMIC (COSV99481689), but in essential thrombocythemia (ET). Missense mutations in codons 1842-1921 of TET2 have been shown to impact the response to hypomethylating agents, including azacitidine and decitabine (NCCN, MDS v1.2023). Additionally, mutations in codons 1842-1921 of TET2 are unfavorably prognostic in myeloproliferative neoplasms (NCCN, MPN v3.2022). While recent analyses in CMML patients demonstrated that TET2 mutations had no significant impact on overall survival (OS), a longer, progression-free survival (PFS) was observed compared to patients with wild-type TET2 (PMID: 27486981, 28476038). Moreover, in CMML patients, TET2 mutations were associated with poor outcomes in the presence of adverse risk gene mutations (including SRSF2), and a decrease in OS and PFS (PMID: 27486981).

A TET2, p.R1359C, missense variant was identified. TET2 is a DNA demethylase and functions as a tumor suppressor. Alterations in TET2 have been associated with several hematological malignancies (PMID: 26099018). Codon 1359 resides in the catalytic double-strand beta helix (DSBH) domain of TET2 and while genetic variations are predicted to be 'Possibly Damaging' by PolyPhen-2, the functional impact of TET2 p.R1359C remains to be determined (PMID: 25132561). TET2 p.R1359C has been reported by COSMIC (COSV54397532) in chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML). Mutations in codons 1344-1444 of TET2 occur in 40-60% of CMML cases and are associated with worsened overall prognosis and an increased rate of leukemic transformation in myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) (NCCN, MDS v1.2023). Furthermore, missense mutations in codons 1344-1444 of TET2 have been shown to impact the response to hypomethylating agents, including azacitidine and decitabine (NCCN, MDS v1.2023). However, while recent analyses in CMML patients demonstrated that TET2 mutations had no significant impact on overall survival (OS), a longer, progression-free survival (PFS) was observed compared to patients with wild-type TET2 (PMID: 27486981, 28476038). Moreover, in CMML patients, TET2 mutations were associated with poor outcomes in the presence of adverse risk gene mutations (including SRSF2), and a decrease in OS and PFS (PMID: 27486981).

An NRAS, p.G12D, missense variant was identified. NRAS is a membrane protein with GTPase activity and codon 12 resides in the GTP-binding region. GTPase domain mutations impair activity leading to unregulated activation of PI3K and MAPK downstream pathways (PMID: 28847905). NRAS p.G12D has been reported in COSMIC (COSV54736383) in chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) and in ClinVar as 'Pathogenic' (Variation ID 39648). Genes frequently somatically mutated in myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) include NRAS and missense mutations (including those at codon 12) are frequently detected in CMML and juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML) at ~15% frequency. These mutations are often associated with a myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN)-like CMML (proliferative) phenotype (NCCN, MDS v3.2021; PMID: 29878489, 27385790). Several gene mutations have been identified among patients with MDS that may, in part, contribute to the clinical heterogeneity of the disease course, and thereby influence the prognosis of patients, including NRAS. Mutations in NRAS have been associated with adverse clinical features including excess bone marrow blast proportion and thrombocytopenia. Constitutional (germline) mutations in NRAS can occur and cause a hematopoietic phenotype. Mutations identified in testing blood or marrow for somatic mutations associated with MDS can identify constitutional (germline) mutations. Distinguishing constitutional from somatic mutations often requires sequencing DNA from a non-hematopoietic tissue in MDS (NCCN, MDS v1.2023).         MEK inhibitor trametinib, an FDA-approved drug for unresectable or metastatic melanoma, showed a 27% overall response rate in RAS-mutated (NRAS or KRAS) CMML patients in a phase I/II trial (PMID 26990290). In CMML patients treated with hypomethylating agents (HMA), mutations in RAS GTPases (including NRAS) had no effect on overall response rate (PMID: 29728305). A study in CMML patients reported that NRAS mutations did not predict response or survival on decitabine therapy (PMID: 21828134). According to 2018 ELN and EHA recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of CMML in adults, hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) may be considered in selected, lower-risk patients with poor prognosis factors that includes poor risk somatic mutations in NRAS (PMID: 31723789). In MDS/MPN patients (including CMML) after hematopoeitic stem cell transplant, mutations (including NRAS) had no impact on the survival outcomes of the patients (PMID: 24164563). However, as per another study in MDS/MPN patients (including CMML), those with detectable mutations (such as NRAS) after HSCT had a higher incidence of relapse than in patients with undetectable mutations (PMID: 28096091). In a cohort of CMML patients who underwent their first allo-HSCT, NRAS mutations were associated with worse overall survival (OS) (PMID: 33755092). Patients with MDS/MPN overlap neoplasms (including CMML) who underwent allogenic HSCT with RAS-pathway mutations (including NRAS p.G12D) had significantly shorter 1-year OS, however no significantly different 5-year OS or non-relapse mortality was observed compared to those without any RAS-pathway mutations (PMID: 32513965).

A SRSF2 p.P95H missense variant was identified. SRSF2 regulates spliceosomal components at both the 5'- and 3'-splice sites during spliceosome assembly. Codon 95 of SRSF2 is a mutational hot spot and genomic alterations may result in mis-splicing of key hematopoietic regulators and impaired hematopoietic differentiation (PMID: 25965569). Mutations in SRSF2 have been reported in chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML), as well as myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), myelofibrosis, and mastocytosis (PMID: 25445211, 22431577). Codon 95 missense mutations in SRSF2 are associated with poor prognosis in CMML (NCCN, MDS v1.2023). The p.P95H alteration has been shown to result in a gain of function, altering RNA-binding affinity and specificity of the SRSF2 RNA recognition motif (PMID: 25965569, 26261309). Pharmacologic modulation of splicing may offer potential treatments for tumors harboring spliceosomal mutations (PMID: 27836865).

A TET2 p.R1179Sfs*46 deletion was identified. This 4 base deletion results in a frameshift alteration and generation of a premature stop codon, subsequent protein truncation and likely loss of function of the TET2 gene product. However, the actual functional impact of TET2 p.R1179Sfs*46 remains to be determined. TET2 is involved in myelopoiesis and alterations in the TET2 gene are associated with several myeloproliferative disorders. Azacitidine and decitabine, both inhibitors of DNA methyltransferases, are FDA-approved for treating patients diagnosed with CMML. While TET2 mutations have been show to impact the response to hypomethylating agents in MDS, TET2 genetic alteration status had no effect on the overall survival of CMML patients who have been treated with hypomethylating agents (NCCN, MDSv1.2023, PMID: 30964202).

A JAK2 p.V617F activating mutation was identified. JAK2 encodes a receptor-associated Janus kinase that plays a central role in cytokine and growth factor signaling. Codon 617 lies within the pseudo-protein tyrosine kinase domain (PMID: 34095761) and results in constitutive activation of JAK2 and its downstream signaling pathways (PMID: 15858187). JAK2 V617F mutations accounts for 60% of patients with ET or MF and more than 90% of patients with PV and the presence of JAK2 V617F is one of the WHO-defined major diagnostic criteria for PV, pre-MF, and overt-MF and ET. It is independently associated with intermediate prognosis and higher risk of thrombosis compared to patients with CALR mutations (NCCN, MPN v3.2022).

A SRSF2 p.P95H missense mutation is identified. Codon P95 in SRSF2 is a hotspot, and mutations (including p.P95H) have been shown to cause mis-splicing of key hematopoietic regulators and impaired hematopoietic differentiation (PMID: 25965569). The SRSF2 gene encodes a member of the Serine/Arginine (SR)-rich family of pre-mRNA splicing factors, which constitute a part of the spliceosome complex. In primary myelofibrosis, SRSF2 mutations are independently associated with inferior OS and leukemia-free survival (NCCN MPN v3.2022). The presence of mutations in genes including SRSF2 was also reported to be >95% specific for the diagnosis of secondary AML (sAML) compared with de novo AML (PMID: 25550361). In a recent study of 2,678 patients with AML, mutations in splicing factor genes (including SRSF2) were associated with inferior relapse-free and overall survival, however these mutations did not represent independent prognostic markers (PMID: 32358566). In AML patients treated with frontline hypomethylating agents and venetoclax–based therapy, spliceosome mutations (including SRSF2) had no impact on overall survival or composite complete response (PMID: 33885753).

A frameshift truncating alteration in ASXL1, E635Rfs*15, is identified. This variant has been well-documented in myeloid neoplasms, including in myeloproliferative neoplasms. ASXL1 is a member of the polycomb group of proteins, which are necessary for the maintenance of stable repression of homeotic and other loci. In primary myelofibrosis, ASXL1 mutations in the absence of CALR mutation are associated with inferior OS (NCCN, MPN v3.2022). In AML, ASXL1 mutations are associated with adverse prognosis independent of karyotype (NCCN AML v2.2022).

A p.L992* nonsense mutation is identified. ASXL1 is a member of the polycomb group of proteins, which are necessary for the maintenance of stable repression of homeotic and other loci. This variant has not been well reported or characterized in the literature or available databases, but as a nonsense mutation resulting in a premature stop codon is predicted to have a deleterious effect on gene function. While not diagnostic of any particular myeloid neoplasm, ASXL1 mutations are commonly identified in chronic myelomonocytic leukemia and myeloproliferative neoplasms where they are associated with adverse prognosis, particularly in primary myelofibrosis and polycythemia vera (NCCN MPN v3.2022). Correlation with clinical and morphologic findings is required for complete interpretation.

A frameshift alteration in CALR, L367Tfs, is identified in this sample. CALR mutations are recurrent in myeloproliferative neoplasms and can be diagnostic in the correct clinical and morphologic context. In primary myelofibrosis, when seen with a concurrent ASXL1 mutation as in this case, they are associated with intermediate prognosis (NCCN MPN v3.2022).

A p.W1037* nonsense mutation is identified. ASXL1 is a member of the polycomb group of proteins, which are necessary for the maintenance of stable repression of homeotic and other loci. This variant has been reported in multiple cases of myeloproliferative neoplasm, as well as other myeloid neoplasm. As a nonsense mutation resulting in a premature stop codon is predicted to have a deleterious effect on gene function and is likely pathogenic in this case. However, this variant is detected at the limit of sensitivity of the assay and may be assay noise. Thus it is conservatively classified in this case. Given the presence of an additional ASXL1 mutation, its inclusion or omission does not affect interpretation of the overall assay results.

A p.P486Sfs*3 mutation is identified. EZH2 encodes the catalytic component of the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), which is responsible for the methylation of lysine 27 on the N-terminal tail of histone H3 (H3K27) and influences stem cell renewal. This variant has not been well reported or characterized in the literature or available databases, but as a frameshift mutation resulting in a premature stop codon is predicted to have a deleterious effect on gene function. While not diagnostic of any particular myeloid neoplasm, EZH2 mutations are commonly identified in many, including myeloproliferative neoplasms where they are associated with adverse prognosis, particularly in primary myelofibrosis and essential thrombocythemia (NCCN MPN v3.2022). Correlation with clinical and morphologic findings is required for complete interpretation.
